entries.meaning: A set of colored lights that tells drivers when to stop and go. ---
examples: Turn left at the second traffic light.
All the traffic lights on Main went out during the storm.
He sat at the traffic light for what felt like ten minutes.

entries.meaning: A line of vehicles that has slowed almost to a stop. ---
examples: We sat in a traffic jam for two hours outside Denver.
There are always traffic jams on the bridge after five.
A stalled truck caused the whole traffic jam.

entries.meaning: An open area where drivers leave their cars. ---
examples: Meet me in the parking lot behind the store.
Both parking lots were full by nine in the morning.
Someone dinged my door in the parking lot.
entries.contrast: Americans say parking lot; the British say car park.

entries.meaning: A place where drivers buy fuel for their vehicles. ---
examples: Pull over at the next gas station.
There are two gas stations at that exit.
The gas station on the corner also sells coffee.
entries.contrast: Americans say gas station; the British say petrol station.

entries.meaning: The official card that allows a person to drive. ---
examples: I got my driver's license the week I turned sixteen.
The officer asked for our driver's licenses and registration.
You need a driver's license or a passport to board.
entries.contrast: American spelling license; the British write driving licence.

entries.meaning: A board beside the road that gives drivers information or orders. ---
examples: The road sign said the bridge was out.
Snow had covered half the road signs.
Slow down and read the road sign.

entries.meaning: A traffic light, in everyday American speech. ---
examples: Take a right at the stoplight.
There are only three stoplights in the whole town.
She stopped for the stoplight and checked her phone.

entries.meaning: The signal that tells drivers to stop. ---
examples: He ran a red light and got a ticket.
We hit every red light between here and the airport.
Wait at the red light until it turns green.

entries.meaning: The signal that tells drivers they may go. ---
examples: The car behind me honked the second I got a green light.
We caught all green lights down Sixth Avenue.
Don't pull out until you have a green light.
entries.contrast: Also used figuratively: to give a project the green light is to approve it.

entries.meaning: A written fine given to a driver who goes too fast. ---
examples: I got a speeding ticket on the way to work.
Two speeding tickets in one year raised his insurance.
The speeding ticket cost me two hundred dollars.

entries.meaning: A fine left on a car that is parked illegally. ---
examples: There was a parking ticket under my wiper.
She has three unpaid parking tickets.
I fought the parking ticket and won.

entries.meaning: A marked area big enough for one parked car. ---
examples: The apartment comes with one parking space.
Half the parking spaces were reserved for staff.
That parking space is too tight for a truck.

entries.meaning: A place where you can leave your car, in everyday speech. ---
examples: I found a parking spot right in front.
Good parking spots fill up fast on game day.
We circled the block twice looking for a parking spot.

entries.meaning: The practice of leaving a car along the side of a public street. ---
examples: There is free street parking after six.
Street parking downtown is almost impossible.
The building has no garage, only street parking.

entries.meaning: The extra brake that holds a parked car still. ---
examples: Set the parking brake before you get out.
Some older cars have parking brakes you pull by hand.
The car rolled because he forgot the parking brake.
entries.contrast: Also called the emergency brake or e-brake in the US; the British say handbrake.

entries.meaning: A stretch of curb reserved for trucks dropping off or picking up goods. ---
examples: You can't leave the car in a loading zone.
Both loading zones were blocked by delivery vans.
He parked in the loading zone for two minutes and got a ticket.

entries.meaning: The edge of the street next to the sidewalk, where cars stop. ---
examples: Leave the trash bins at the curbside Sunday night.
The restaurant added curbside pickup last year.
She waited at the curbside with two suitcases.
entries.contrast: American curb; the British spell the same thing kerb.

entries.meaning: Someone who parks your car for you at a hotel or restaurant. ---
examples: The valet brought the car around in five minutes.
Two valets were working the front entrance.
Hand your keys to the valet and take the ticket.
entries.contrast: In American usage the final t is silent and the stress falls on the second syllable: va-LAY.

entries.meaning: The fenced yard where the city keeps cars it has towed away. ---
examples: His car spent the weekend in the impound lot.
The city runs two impound lots on the south side.
Getting a car out of the impound lot costs a fortune.

entries.meaning: The pulling away of a vehicle by a truck, usually because it broke down or parked illegally. ---
examples: The sign warns that towing is enforced at all hours.
Towing is covered by my roadside plan.
The bill included ninety dollars for towing.
entries.contrast: Tow rhymes with go and sounds like toe, never like cow.

entries.meaning: A street where traffic is allowed to move in only one direction. ---
examples: You just turned the wrong way onto a one-way street.
Most of the one-way streets downtown run north.
That block is a one-way street now.

entries.meaning: A small quiet street leading off a main road. ---
examples: Park on a side street and walk over.
He knows all the side streets around the stadium.
The cafe is on a side street behind the library.

entries.meaning: A street that is closed at one end so cars cannot drive through. ---
examples: Our street is a dead end, so there's no through traffic.
The GPS sent us down two dead ends.
There's a sign at the corner warning that it's a dead end.

entries.meaning: A small country road away from the main highways. ---
examples: We took a back road to avoid the holiday traffic.
He grew up driving these back roads.
The back road adds twenty minutes but it's prettier.

entries.meaning: A road with no pavement, just packed earth. ---
examples: The cabin is at the end of a dirt road.
Dirt roads turn to mud after a heavy rain.
Take the dirt road past the red barn.

entries.meaning: A small road running alongside a highway that reaches the businesses on it. ---
examples: The motel is on the service road, not the freeway itself.
Both service roads were closed for repaving.
Get off at the exit and follow the service road north.
entries.contrast: In parts of the US the same road is called a frontage road.

entries.meaning: The part of a road that vehicles actually drive on. ---
examples: A fallen tree blocked the entire roadway.
Crews salt the roadways before an ice storm.
Keep pedestrians off the roadway.

entries.meaning: The strip of ground along the edge of a road. ---
examples: We pulled over and ate lunch by the roadside.
Wildflowers grow along the roadsides in May.
A deer stood at the roadside watching us pass.

entries.meaning: A road that drivers must pay to use. ---
examples: The toll road saves half an hour.
Several toll roads now charge you by camera.
I avoid the toll road when I'm not in a hurry.

entries.meaning: The small building where drivers pay to use a road or bridge. ---
examples: Slow down before the toll booth.
Half the toll booths are unmanned now.
He rolled down the window at the toll booth.

entries.meaning: Bypass has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Take the bypass and skip downtown altogether.
The two new bypasses cut travel time in half.
The bypass was built in the seventies.
He had a triple bypass last spring.
Bypass surgery kept her in the hospital for a week.
The doctor recommended a bypass rather than a stent.

senses.head: A road built around a town so traffic does not have to go through it
examples: Take the bypass and skip downtown altogether.
The two new bypasses cut travel time in half.
The bypass was built in the seventies.

senses.head: An operation that routes blood around a blocked artery of the heart
examples: He had a triple bypass last spring.
Bypass surgery kept her in the hospital for a week.
The doctor recommended a bypass rather than a stent.

entries.meaning: A highway that circles a city. ---
examples: Traffic on the beltway is brutal at rush hour.
Several cities have built outer beltways.
We live just inside the beltway.
entries.contrast: Americans say beltway; the British say ring road.

entries.meaning: The short road used to drive onto a highway. ---
examples: Get up to speed on the on-ramp.
Both on-ramps were backed up to the light.
A truck stalled on the on-ramp.
entries.contrast: Americans say on-ramp and off-ramp; the British call both a slip road.

entries.meaning: The short road used to drive off a highway. ---
examples: Take the next off-ramp and turn right.
Two off-ramps were closed for construction.
He braked hard at the top of the off-ramp.

entries.meaning: The place where two highways cross and drivers can move from one to the other. ---
examples: Stay in the right lane through the interchange.
The city is rebuilding three interchanges this summer.
That interchange confuses everyone the first time.
entries.contrast: The noun stresses the first syllable, IN-tur-chaynj; the verb interchange stresses the last.

entries.meaning: A round junction that traffic drives around instead of stopping. ---
examples: Take the second exit off the traffic circle.
The town put in two traffic circles to slow drivers down.
I always miss my turn at that traffic circle.
entries.contrast: Americans say traffic circle, or rotary in New England; the British say roundabout.

entries.meaning: A crossing where every direction must stop and cars go in the order they arrived. ---
examples: It's a four-way stop, so whoever got there first goes first.
There are four-way stops on every corner in that neighborhood.
Nobody knew whose turn it was at the four-way stop.
entries.русский: перекрёсток со знаком «стоп» на всех подъездах

entries.meaning: The place where a road runs across a train track. ---
examples: The gates came down at the railroad crossing.
There are three railroad crossings between here and town.
School buses stop at every railroad crossing.
entries.contrast: Americans say railroad crossing; the British say level crossing.

entries.meaning: A raised area in the middle of a road that separates lanes or shelters people crossing. ---
examples: Wait on the traffic island if the light changes.
They planted flowers on the traffic islands.
Her front tire clipped the traffic island.
entries.contrast: The s in island is silent: EYE-luhnd.

entries.meaning: A grooved strip on the road edge that makes a loud noise when tires cross it. ---
examples: The rumble strip woke him up in time.
Rumble strips run along both shoulders of the highway.
You could hear the tires hit the rumble strip.

entries.meaning: A small roadside sign showing the distance along a highway. ---
examples: The wreck is near mile marker 42.
Mile markers count up as you drive north.
Watch for the mile marker and turn just past it.

entries.meaning: A place beside a highway with parking and restrooms where drivers can stop. ---
examples: Let's pull into the next rest area.
The rest areas on this stretch are twenty miles apart.
We slept an hour at a rest area outside Amarillo.

entries.meaning: A roadside stop where trucks are weighed and checked. ---
examples: The weigh station was closed, so he drove on.
There are two weigh stations on this route.
Every loaded truck has to pull into the weigh station.
entries.contrast: The gh is silent: weigh sounds exactly like way.

entries.meaning: A longer, prettier road taken instead of the fastest one. ---
examples: We took the scenic route along the coast.
The map marks the scenic routes in green.
The scenic route costs you an hour but it's worth it.
entries.contrast: Americans say route as either ROOT or ROWT; both are standard.

entries.meaning: A long journey made by car for pleasure. ---
examples: We're taking a road trip to the Grand Canyon.
Their summer road trips covered half the country.
A good playlist makes the road trip.

entries.meaning: The lane used to get around slower vehicles. ---
examples: Don't sit in the passing lane.
The highway adds passing lanes on the long hills.
He pulled into the passing lane and floored it.

entries.meaning: The left lane, where the quickest traffic moves. ---
examples: Move over if you're not using the fast lane.
Even the fast lanes were crawling this morning.
She stayed in the fast lane the whole way.

entries.meaning: A lane reserved for vehicles carrying more than one person. ---
examples: You need two people to use the carpool lane.
The carpool lanes move twice as fast at rush hour.
He got fined for driving alone in the carpool lane.

entries.meaning: A lane set aside for cars turning off the road. ---
examples: Get in the left turn lane early.
The intersection has turn lanes in both directions.
The turn lane was full, so I missed the light.

entries.meaning: A lane that only buses are allowed to drive in. ---
examples: Cars can't drive in the bus lane on weekdays.
The city painted the new bus lanes bright red.
A camera catches anyone using the bus lane.

entries.meaning: A path for bicycles, separate from the road. ---
examples: A bike path runs along the river.
The city keeps adding bike paths.
Take the bike path instead of the highway shoulder.

entries.meaning: The blocking of one lane, usually for repairs. ---
examples: A lane closure is causing a two-mile backup.
Expect lane closures overnight while they repave.
The lane closure ends past the bridge.

entries.meaning: The move a driver makes from one lane into another. ---
examples: Signal before every lane change.
He made three lane changes in a hundred yards.
That lane change nearly cut me off.

entries.meaning: The area beside a car that the driver cannot see in the mirrors. ---
examples: Check your blind spot before you merge.
Big trucks have huge blind spots.
She was sitting right in my blind spot.

entries.meaning: The legal right to go first at a junction or crossing. ---
examples: Pedestrians have the right of way in a crosswalk.
The two rights of way were unclear at that corner.
He took the right of way that wasn't his.
entries.contrast: The plural pluralizes the first word: rights of way, not right of ways.

entries.meaning: A turn that takes a car back the way it came. ---
examples: Make a U-turn at the next light.
U-turns are illegal on this stretch.
He missed the driveway and made a U-turn.

entries.meaning: Turning a car around on a narrow street in a forward, backward, forward move. ---
examples: The examiner asked me to do a three-point turn.
Three-point turns are hard in a long truck.
She managed a three-point turn on a very narrow road.

entries.meaning: Backing a car into a space along the curb between two other cars. ---
examples: Parallel parking is the part of the test everybody dreads.
He's still not comfortable with parallel parking.
The instructor spent an hour on parallel parking.

entries.meaning: Reverse has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Put it in reverse and back out slowly.
The car rolled forward because it wasn't in reverse.
Reverse grinds a little in this old truck.
I thought he'd be angry, but the reverse was true.
The order of names is the reverse of last year's.
Far from helping, it did the reverse.
The reverse of the quarter shows an eagle.
Sign your name on the reverse of the check.
The date is stamped on the reverse.

senses.head: The gear that makes a vehicle move backward
examples: Put it in reverse and back out slowly.
The car rolled forward because it wasn't in reverse.
Reverse grinds a little in this old truck.

senses.head: The opposite of what has just been said or expected
examples: I thought he'd be angry, but the reverse was true.
The order of names is the reverse of last year's.
Far from helping, it did the reverse.

senses.head: The back side of a coin, medal, or sheet of paper
examples: The reverse of the quarter shows an eagle.
Sign your name on the reverse of the check.
The date is stamped on the reverse.

entries.русский: задний ход; противоположность, обратное; оборотная сторона, реверс

entries.meaning: A triangular sign telling drivers to let other traffic go first. ---
examples: There's a yield sign where the ramp joins the road.
Yield signs are red and white triangles here.
He blew through the yield sign without slowing.
entries.contrast: The American yield sign is a give way sign in Britain.

entries.meaning: A person who stops traffic so children can cross the street. ---
examples: The crossing guard held up her stop sign.
Two crossing guards work that corner every morning.
Wait for the crossing guard to wave you across.

entries.meaning: The stretch of road near a school where the speed limit drops. ---
examples: Fines are doubled in a school zone.
The city lowered the limit in all school zones.
Slow to twenty through the school zone.

entries.meaning: A part of the road where work is going on and traffic is restricted. ---
examples: Traffic crawls through the construction zone.
There are two construction zones between here and the state line.
Speeding fines double in a construction zone.

entries.meaning: Repair or building work being done on a road. ---
examples: There's road work ahead for the next three miles.
Road work on the bridge starts Monday.
The delay was caused by road work, not an accident.
entries.contrast: Also written roadwork; the British say roadworks and treat it as plural.

entries.meaning: A road worker who signals drivers to stop or go through a work area. ---
examples: The flagger held us for five minutes.
Two flaggers were working each end of the lane.
Watch for the flagger around the curve.

entries.meaning: A place where police wait to catch drivers going too fast. ---
examples: That hill is a well-known speed trap.
The little town is famous for its speed traps.
He warned me about the speed trap past the bridge.

entries.meaning: A roadside camera that photographs cars going over the limit. ---
examples: A speed camera caught him doing sixty in a thirty-five.
The city installed speed cameras near the schools.
The ticket came from a speed camera, not an officer.

entries.meaning: A police officer who patrols the highways of a state. ---
examples: A state trooper pulled us over near the state line.
Two state troopers were directing traffic around the crash.
The state trooper let him off with a warning.

entries.meaning: The police force responsible for traffic on a state's highways. ---
examples: Call the highway patrol if you see a stalled car.
Neighboring highway patrols worked the same storm.
The highway patrol closed the road for three hours.

entries.meaning: A traffic offense committed while the vehicle is moving, such as speeding. ---
examples: Running that stop sign is a moving violation.
Two moving violations can raise your rates.
A parking ticket is not a moving violation.

entries.meaning: The court that hears cases about driving offenses. ---
examples: I have to be in traffic court on Thursday.
County traffic courts handle thousands of tickets a month.
The judge in traffic court cut the fine in half.
entries.русский: суд по делам о нарушениях ПДД

entries.meaning: A short course a driver takes to keep a ticket off the record. ---
examples: I took traffic school online in one evening.
The judge offered him traffic school instead of points.
Traffic school cost less than the fine.

entries.meaning: A device that measures alcohol in a driver's breath. ---
examples: He refused to blow into the breathalyzer.
Every patrol car carries a breathalyzer.
The breathalyzer read twice the legal limit.
entries.contrast: American spelling breathalyzer with a z; the British write breathalyser.

entries.meaning: A roadside check of whether a driver has been drinking. ---
examples: The officer gave him a sobriety test on the shoulder.
Field sobriety tests include walking a straight line.
She passed the sobriety test easily.

entries.meaning: Driving after drinking too much alcohol. ---
examples: Drunk driving costs him his license for a year.
The state cracked down on drunk driving.
He was arrested for drunk driving twice.

entries.meaning: Driving while paying attention to a phone or something else instead of the road. ---
examples: Distracted driving causes more crashes every year.
Texting at the wheel counts as distracted driving.
The campaign is aimed at teenage distracted driving.

entries.meaning: A way of driving that expects other people's mistakes and leaves room for them. ---
examples: His insurance dropped after a defensive driving course.
Defensive driving means always having an escape route.
They teach defensive driving to every new hire.

entries.meaning: Someone who crosses the street away from a crosswalk or against the light. ---
examples: A jaywalker stepped right out in front of me.
Jaywalkers rarely get ticketed here.
The driver swerved around a jaywalker.

entries.meaning: Traffic so blocked in every direction that nothing can move. ---
examples: The parade turned downtown into total gridlock.
Gridlock starts around four every weekday.
One broken light caused an hour of gridlock.

entries.meaning: The condition of roads being too full of vehicles. ---
examples: Congestion on the bridge gets worse every year.
The new lanes did nothing for congestion.
Traffic apps route you around congestion.

entries.meaning: A narrow point where traffic slows and backs up. ---
examples: The tunnel is the worst bottleneck in the city.
Two bottlenecks on this route add half an hour.
They widened the road to fix the bottleneck.

entries.meaning: A complete stop of traffic or other movement. ---
examples: The freeway came to a standstill after the crash.
Snow brought the city to a standstill.
Two standstills in one morning is unusual.

entries.meaning: A short broadcast telling drivers where the delays are. ---
examples: The traffic report said the bridge was backed up.
Traffic reports run every ten minutes on that station.
I always check the traffic report before I leave.

entries.meaning: Driving too close behind the car in front. ---
examples: Tailgating causes most rear-end crashes.
He slowed down to discourage the tailgating.
The trooper pulled her over for tailgating.
entries.русский: езда вплотную за впереди идущей машиной
entries.contrast: In the US tailgating also means a parking-lot party before a football game.

entries.meaning: Angry, aggressive behavior by a driver toward other drivers. ---
examples: The argument on the freeway was pure road rage.
Road rage incidents rise in hot weather.
He was charged after a road rage incident.

entries.meaning: The exam a person must pass to get a license. ---
examples: She failed her driving test the first time.
Driving tests are booked out for a month.
I passed the driving test on my second try.

entries.meaning: The behind-the-wheel part of a driving exam. ---
examples: My road test is scheduled for Friday morning.
They give road tests only on weekdays.
He passed the written part but not the road test.

entries.meaning: A business that teaches people to drive. ---
examples: My parents signed me up for driving school.
There are three driving schools in town.
The driving school provides the car for the test.

entries.meaning: A person who teaches learners how to drive. ---
examples: My driving instructor had nerves of steel.
Driving instructors have their own brake pedal.
The driving instructor told me to relax my grip.

entries.meaning: One session of learning to drive with a teacher. ---
examples: I have a driving lesson after school.
Ten driving lessons came with the package.
The first driving lesson was just parking lot circles.

entries.meaning: A document that lets a beginner drive with a licensed adult in the car. ---
examples: He got his learner's permit at fifteen.
Learner's permits are good for one year here.
With a learner's permit you can't drive alone.

entries.meaning: The class in which American teenagers learn the rules of the road. ---
examples: We watched crash videos in driver's ed.
Driver's ed is offered every summer at the high school.
She takes driver's ed on Tuesday nights.
entries.contrast: Short for driver's education; almost always said the short way.

entries.meaning: A person learning to drive, often marked by a sign on the car. ---
examples: Give that car room; it says student driver.
Student drivers practice in this lot on Saturdays.
The student driver stalled twice at the light.
entries.contrast: Americans say STOO-duhnt; the British say STYOO-duhnt.

entries.meaning: The official history of a person's tickets and crashes. ---
examples: He has a clean driving record.
The company checks driving records before it hires.
One ticket stays on your driving record for three years.
entries.contrast: The noun is REK-urd; the verb record is rih-KORD, with the stress moved.

entries.meaning: Any road vehicle with an engine, in official language. ---
examples: You register a motor vehicle at the county office.
No motor vehicles are allowed on the trail.
The law applies to every motor vehicle on public roads.
entries.contrast: The h in vehicle is silent: VEE-uh-kuhl.

entries.meaning: A car, in formal or written English. ---
examples: The automobile changed how American cities were built.
Automobiles were still rare in 1910.
He worked forty years in the automobile industry.
entries.contrast: Formal and mostly written; in speech Americans just say car.

entries.meaning: A car trip booked through a phone app with a private driver. ---
examples: We took a rideshare home from the airport.
Rideshares are cheaper than cabs here.
My rideshare is four minutes away.

entries.meaning: An uncontrolled slide of a vehicle on the road. ---
examples: The car went into a skid on the wet curve.
Long skids were visible on the pavement.
Steer into the skid, not against it.

entries.meaning: Sliding on a film of water because the tires have lost contact with the road. ---
examples: Hydroplaning is the danger in heavy rain.
Worn tires make hydroplaning much more likely.
He lost control to hydroplaning at highway speed.
entries.contrast: Americans say hydroplaning; the British say aquaplaning.

entries.meaning: A thin clear layer of ice on the road that drivers cannot see. ---
examples: The bridge was covered in black ice.
Black ice forms fast after sundown.
Three cars spun out on black ice that morning.

entries.meaning: How far a vehicle travels between the brakes going on and the car stopping. ---
examples: Rain doubles your stopping distance.
Stopping distances are longer for loaded trucks.
At seventy the stopping distance is the length of a football field.

entries.meaning: The gap a driver keeps behind the vehicle in front. ---
examples: Keep a safe following distance in the rain.
Following distances shrink as traffic gets heavy.
Three seconds is a decent following distance.

entries.meaning: A tire that has lost its air. ---
examples: I got a flat tire two miles from home.
Two flat tires in one month is bad luck.
He changed the flat tire in the rain.
entries.contrast: American tire; the British spell it tyre and often say puncture.

entries.meaning: Starting a car with a dead battery using power from another car. ---
examples: Can you give me a jump start?
The cold morning meant three jump starts in the lot.
A quick jump start got the van going.

entries.meaning: A service that comes to help drivers who break down. ---
examples: Call roadside assistance and wait in the car.
Roadside assistance is included with the insurance.
Roadside assistance took an hour to reach us.

entries.meaning: How much air is inside a vehicle's tires. ---
examples: Check your tire pressure before a long trip.
Cold weather drops the tire pressure.
The light came on because the tire pressure was low.

entries.meaning: The machine at a station that puts fuel into a vehicle. ---
examples: Pull up to the gas pump on the far side.
All six gas pumps were busy.
The gas pump wouldn't take my card.

entries.meaning: The lid that closes the opening of a fuel tank. ---
examples: He drove off and left the gas cap on the roof.
Replacement gas caps cost about ten dollars.
A loose gas cap can trigger the warning light.

entries.meaning: How far a vehicle can travel on a certain amount of fuel. ---
examples: This truck gets terrible gas mileage.
Highway driving improves your gas mileage.
Gas mileage was the first thing she asked about.

entries.meaning: The routine service of draining old engine oil and putting in new. ---
examples: The car is due for an oil change.
Two oil changes a year is plenty for me.
The oil change took twenty minutes.

entries.meaning: A service that adjusts an engine so it runs properly. ---
examples: The van needs a tune-up before the trip.
Regular tune-ups keep an old car alive.
A tune-up fixed the rough idle.
entries.contrast: Americans say TOON; the British say TYOON.

entries.meaning: The adjustment of the wheels so the car runs straight. ---
examples: The pothole ruined my wheel alignment.
Wheel alignments are cheap compared to new tires.
Get a wheel alignment if the car pulls to one side.

entries.meaning: A check of how much pollution a vehicle's exhaust produces. ---
examples: The car failed its emissions test.
Some states require emissions tests every two years.
You can't renew the tags without an emissions test.

entries.meaning: A place or machine that cleans vehicles. ---
examples: Run it through the car wash on the way home.
Two new car washes opened on that road.
The car wash broke my antenna.

entries.meaning: A garage that repairs damaged car bodies and paint. ---
examples: The body shop said it would take a week.
Insurance keeps a list of approved body shops.
My car is still at the body shop.

entries.meaning: A short drive taken to see whether you want to buy a car. ---
examples: Take it for a test drive before you decide.
We did three test drives in one afternoon.
The test drive sold him on the car.

entries.meaning: A car that has had an earlier owner. ---
examples: Her first used car cost two thousand dollars.
Used cars got expensive after the shortage.
Have a mechanic look at any used car first.
entries.contrast: Here used ends in a z sound, /juːzd/; in used to it is /juːst/, with an s.

entries.meaning: The mirror on the outside of a car door. ---
examples: A truck clipped my side mirror.
Fold the side mirrors in before the car wash.
Adjust the side mirror before you pull out.
entries.contrast: Americans say side mirror; the British say wing mirror.

entries.meaning: The red light at the back of a car that comes on when the driver brakes. ---
examples: Your left brake light is out.
A wall of brake lights appeared ahead of us.
The brake light costs a few dollars to replace.
entries.contrast: Brake sounds exactly like break but is spelled with a-k-e.

entries.meaning: The blinking lights a driver turns on to warn others of trouble. ---
examples: Put your hazard lights on if you stop on the shoulder.
His hazard lights were flashing in the breakdown lane.
She left the hazard lights going while she changed the tire.
entries.contrast: Used only in the plural; also called flashers in everyday speech.

entries.meaning: The brightest setting of a car's headlights, for empty dark roads. ---
examples: Turn off your high beams when a car comes toward you.
The high beams lit up the whole field.
He flashed his high beams to warn us.
entries.contrast: Used only in the plural; the British say full beam or main beam.

entries.meaning: The dial showing how much fuel is left in the tank. ---
examples: The fuel gauge has been stuck on full for a week.
Old fuel gauges are not very accurate.
Keep an eye on the fuel gauge out here.
entries.contrast: Gauge is pronounced GAYJ despite the spelling.

entries.meaning: The warning lamp on the dashboard that says the engine needs attention. ---
examples: The check engine light came on again this morning.
Check engine lights can mean almost anything.
He drove for months with the check engine light on.

entries.meaning: The system that holds a car at a set speed without the driver pressing the pedal. ---
examples: I set the cruise control at seventy.
Don't use cruise control on icy roads.
The rental car has cruise control and a backup camera.

entries.meaning: The small remote that locks, unlocks and often starts a car. ---
examples: The battery in my key fob died.
Both key fobs came with the car.
Press the key fob twice to unlock all the doors.

entries.meaning: A small camera mounted on the windshield that records the road. ---
examples: The dash cam caught the whole thing.
Dash cams have gotten cheap.
Insurance asked for the dash cam footage.

entries.meaning: A printed map showing the roads of an area. ---
examples: There's an old road map in the glove compartment.
Gas stations used to give away road maps.
He unfolded the road map across the hood.

entries.meaning: The flap above the windshield that a driver folds down against the sun. ---
examples: Flip the sun visor down, the glare is awful.
Both sun visors have little mirrors.
The parking pass clips to the sun visor.

entries.meaning: The system that clears ice or fog from a car's windows. ---
examples: Turn on the defroster before you pull out.
The rear defroster stopped working.
Old cars had weak defrosters.
entries.contrast: Americans say defroster; the British say demister.

entries.meaning: The seat behind the driver and front passenger. ---
examples: Throw your bag in the back seat.
The back seats fold down for cargo.
The kids fought in the back seat the whole way.

entries.meaning: The front seat next to the driver. ---
examples: My coffee is in the cup holder by the passenger seat.
Both passenger seats were full of groceries.
He rode in the passenger seat and navigated.

entries.meaning: A sticker with a slogan that a driver puts on the back of a car.
examples: Her car is covered in bumper stickers.
The bumper sticker made me laugh at the red light.
He peeled the old bumper sticker off before selling it.
